abstract: Phosphate (Pi) limitation is a major constraint on plant productivity and is aggravated by heat stress. In nature, soil buffers air temperature, creating a vertical thermal gradient that shields roots from extreme heat; thus, heat and Pi starvation, although often co-occurring, are perceived mainly by different organs, shoots and roots respectively. How plants integrate these organ-specific stresses into a coordinated response remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how Arabidopsis responds to combined Pi deficiency and elevated temperature, using a root-zone temperature gradient and an integrated analysis of ion accumulation, phytohormone levels and transcriptomic profiles in roots and shoots. The combined stress elicited a distinct response that cannot be explained by the addition of individual stress effects. Jasmonate levels changed in an organ-specific manner, with JA-Ile accumulating in roots and JA declining in shoots, and mutants with reduced (jar1-1) or constitutive (jazQ) JA signaling showed altered transcriptional, growth and leaf-temperature responses. These results identify jasmonic acid (JA) as a modulator of the balance between acclimation and growth under combined nutritional and thermal limitation, advancing our understanding of how plants cope with the multi-stress scenarios driven by climate change.
